title: Turkey Joins Saudi-Led Red Sea Coalition, Fidan Meets Hamas as Israel Slams Ankara, Wildfires Hit Tourist Coast
subhead: Ankara signs onto a 14-nation maritime coalition to protect Red Sea shipping — a notable subordination to Saudi leadership — while FM Fidan's meeting with Hamas's new leader draws sharp Israeli condemnation. At home, wildfires continue to ravage the Aegean and Mediterranean coasts, and the opposition shakeout continues as Davutoglu's exit clears the field for Ozel's Yeni Parti.

sections.heading: Turkey Joins Saudi-Led Red Sea Coalition in Regional Shift
sections.body:
Turkey has signed on as a founding member of a 14-nation maritime defense coalition led by Saudi Arabia to protect Red Sea shipping routes, according to Al-Monitor and Jang News. The coalition — which also includes Kuwait, Qatar, Bahrain, Egypt, Jordan, Pakistan, Djibouti, Somalia, Bangladesh, Yemen, Sudan, and Nigeria — will be headquartered in Riyadh with a joint operations center.

The alliance focuses on securing the Bab el-Mandeb Strait and Gulf of Aden, vital corridors for global oil and trade flows that have been disrupted by Houthi attacks since 2024. Saudi Arabia hosted delegates from 43 countries and the EU for the founding meeting, though the US has not yet signed on and most invitees remain non-committal, according to Al-Monitor.

Turkey's participation is notable because Ankara has historically been reluctant to accept a subordinate role — particularly under a former Ottoman dominion like Saudi Arabia. Al-Monitor reported that the decision 'came as quite a surprise' to diplomatic sources, given Turkey's usual insistence on leadership in international military arrangements. Houthi leader Abdul-Malik al-Houthi warned Saudi Arabia of 'full escalation' in response to the coalition's formation.
sections.whyItMatters: Turkey joining a Saudi-led coalition rather than leading its own marks a pragmatic shift — Ankara is prioritizing maritime security for its trade routes over prestige. But the move also deepens Turkey's stake in the Red Sea theater at a time when the US-Iran conflict has made the Gulf and Red Sea both battleground and bargaining chip.

sections.heading: Fidan Meets Hamas Leadership, Drawing Israeli Condemnation
sections.body:
Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan met with a Hamas delegation in Ankara this week led by the group's new leader, drawing sharp criticism from Israeli Minister of Diaspora Affairs Amichai Chikli, who slammed the meeting on Friday, according to MSN and multiple outlets.

The meeting came in the same week that President Trump announced a Hamas disarmament framework — which Hamas said it would pursue conditional on Israel halting all military operations in Gaza and fulfilling provisions of the October 2025 ceasefire deal. Hamas described the proposal as covering 'police weapons, heavy weapons, military production sites, weapons depots and tunnels, personal weapons and the weapons of militias,' according to Yahoo News.

For Turkey, the Fidan-Hamas meeting is consistent with Ankara's long-standing position of maintaining open channels to the group while publicly advocating for a two-state solution. But the optics are uncomfortable: the same week Trump is pressing a disarmament deal, Turkey is hosting Hamas's leadership — a juxtaposition that Israeli officials seized on to argue, as the State Department noted in its F-35 letter, that Hamas continues to use financial channels operating from Turkish territory.
sections.whyItMatters: The Fidan-Hamas meeting reinforces Turkey's self-image as a regional mediator but provides ammunition to opponents of F-35 sales and other defense cooperation in Washington and Tel Aviv. The timing alongside the Trump-backed disarmament framework makes the optics worse than usual.

sections.heading: Erdogan Offers Troops for Post-UNIFIL Lebanon Force
sections.body:
President Erdogan told visiting Lebanese President Joseph Aoun on Thursday that Turkey is willing to participate in a new security arrangement for southern Lebanon after UNIFIL's mandate expires at the end of 2026, multiple outlets reported. Aoun's visit — the first presidential-level visit from Lebanon to Turkey in 17 years — also covered expanded bilateral cooperation in institutional development, humanitarian aid, and reconstruction.

Erdogan condemned Israeli military operations in Lebanon, citing more than 4,300 Lebanese killed and over one million displaced. He also offered to facilitate further dialogue between Lebanon and Syria.

However, the Middle East Institute's Gonul Tol argued that Turkey's interest stems from its stakes in Syria and the Eastern Mediterranean, while the Stimson Center's Randa Slim countered that Israel will make sure no Turkish forces are deployed in Lebanon, Al-Monitor reported. France and Italy have also expressed interest in contributing to a post-UNIFIL force.
sections.whyItMatters: Turkey's Lebanon offer pairs with its Red Sea coalition membership to show Ankara expanding its military footprint across the Eastern Mediterranean — but the Lebanon proposal faces an immediate Israeli veto. The real value may be diplomatic leverage rather than deployment.

sections.heading: Wildfires Continue Across Western Turkey as Firefighting Stretches Resources
sections.body:
Wildfires continued to burn across western and southern Turkey on Friday, with five active blazes still out of control out of 206 fires recorded since Wednesday, according to Agence France-Presse and MSN. By Friday, 202 of the fires had been brought under control, but strong winds of 50-60 km/h caused several hotspots to reignite — including near Fethiye on the southwest coast and Ayvalik in the northwest.

In Balikesir Province (Ayvalik, Burhaniye, and Gomec), five people were injured — including three firefighters, a forestry official, and a civilian — and three villages were evacuated alongside 720 cattle. In Mugla's Seydikemer district, 408 homes were evacuated, 703 residents relocated, and 55 buildings damaged. In Antalya's Kas district, fires forced the temporary closure of the ancient city of Olympos and the Fethiye-Antalya highway, AFP reported.

Agriculture and Forestry Minister Ibrahim Yumakli said more than 25 firefighting aircraft, 410 ground vehicles, and 1,100+ personnel were deployed to the Mugla blaze alone. Emergency text message alerts were sent to residents in high-risk zones across the south and west.
sections.whyItMatters: These fires hit Turkey's Mediterranean and Aegean tourism corridor at peak season. With the Fethiye-Marmaris-Antalya stretch being the economic backbone of coastal tourism, prolonged disruption would carry outsize economic consequences — especially at a time when the lira is already at record lows.

sections.heading: Opposition Shakeout: Davutoglu Exits as Yeni Parti Consolidates
sections.body:
Former Prime Minister Ahmet Davutoglu announced he is stepping away from party politics and dissolving his Gelecek (Future) Party, according to MSN, completing a process that began earlier in the week. Davutoglu, who founded Gelecek in 2019 after breaking with Erdogan's AKP, never translated his foreign policy stature into electoral success.

His exit accelerates a broader opposition consolidation: Ozgur Ozel's Yeni Parti now has 91 lawmakers in the 600-seat parliament, making it the second-largest party behind the AKP's 277, while the rump CHP under Kemal Kilicdaroglu retains just 44 seats. Opinion polls continue to show Yeni Parti outperforming: a Gundemar Research survey puts Yeni Parti at 34.9% — ahead of the AKP at 30.4% — with Kilicdaroglu's CHP at just 4.3%. A more conservative AREA Research poll shows Yeni Parti at 19.4%, AKP at 34.2%, and CHP at 11.8%, according to Business Turkey Today.

Writing in the Guardian, novelist Kaya Genc argued that 'if managed well, the ousting of Ozel from the CHP will probably boost the popularity of Turkey's progressives overall,' noting the historical pattern of politicians benefiting from legal persecution — including Erdogan himself, who spent four months in prison in 1999 before winning power four years later.
sections.whyItMatters: Davutoglu's departure removes the last prominent AKP dissident with his own party platform. The opposition field is now simpler but more fragmented: Yeni Parti has momentum and parliamentary weight, but a divided opposition in a presidential race could still hand Erdogan a first-round victory.

sections.heading: PKK Amnesty Bill Stalls as Government and Kurds Disagree on Terms
sections.body:
Last-minute negotiations between the government and Kurdish leaders over a draft amnesty law for PKK fighters and prisoners remain deadlocked, Al-Monitor reported. The legislation — which would expunge thousands of PKK-related convictions — is being pushed by AKP spokesperson Omer Celik, who said this week it would be brought to parliament before the legislative recess this month.

But points of disagreement abound. The government reckons it can impose its will because the Kurds hold a weaker hand, according to Al-Monitor. Key sticking points include the scope of amnesty (whether it covers only fighters or also political prisoners convicted of PKK links), the mechanism for demobilization and disarmament, and the fate of imprisoned PKK leader Abdullah Ocalan.

Erdogan is reportedly of two minds about the law, worried about blowback from his nationalist base, who continue to view the PKK and Ocalan as 'baby killers.' Meanwhile, Iraq's powerful judicial council president Faiq Zeidan met with Erdogan on Thursday — a day after Iraqi PM al-Zaidi's visit — in a meeting that may have been connected to Baghdad's potential role in demobilizing and disarming PKK fighters based in northern Iraq.
sections.whyItMatters: The amnesty bill is the legislative centerpiece of Erdogan's 'terror-free Turkey' initiative, but the government's willingness to force terms may produce a law that Kurdish politicians cannot sell to their base — defeating the purpose. Zeidan's visit suggests Ankara is looking to Baghdad for help with the disarmament mechanics, but that only works if the political terms are acceptable to the PKK itself.

sections.heading: Iraq-Turkey Oil Flows Continue on Temporary Extension as Old Treaty Expires
sections.body:
Crude oil flows from northern Iraq to Turkey's Ceyhan port are expected to continue while both countries negotiate a 12-month extension of the bilateral pipeline agreement, according to Reuters. The decades-old 1973 Iraq-Turkey Crude Oil Pipeline Agreement expired on July 27 without Iraqi PM al-Zaidi signing a renewal during his Ankara visit.

Turkish Energy Minister Alparslan Bayraktar announced the 12-month extension agreement, and Erdogan said Turkey hopes to finalize a comprehensive energy cooperation deal soon. The pipeline currently carries approximately 170,000 barrels per day — far below its 1.5 million bpd capacity. A Forbes analysis by Guven Yildiz noted that the expired 1973 treaty was 'the legal battlefield' of the Kurdistan Regional Government's independent marketing fight, and any new framework must be written under the shadow of a prior ICC ruling that found Turkey had breached pipeline agreements.

Turkey's concrete gain from the Zaidi visit is TPAO's 15% stake in BP Energy Company of Kirkuk Limited, alongside BP at 43% and ConocoPhillips at 42%, covering more than 3 billion barrels of oil equivalent. But as Yildiz argues, 'fifteen percent is not control — it is incorporation.' Iraq also offered to supply Turkey with up to 1 million barrels of oil per day, though no formal agreement on that volume has been signed.
sections.whyItMatters: The Kirkuk-Ceyhan pipeline is operating in a legal grey zone covered only by a temporary extension. Turkey's real play is not the transit revenue — it's the TPAO equity stake that transforms Ankara from a pipeline toll-collector into an upstream partner in Iraqi oil.

bottomLine: Turkey expanded its military footprint in two directions this week — joining a Saudi-led Red Sea maritime coalition and offering troops for a post-UNIFIL Lebanon force — while at home, wildfires scorched the tourist coast and the opposition consolidation accelerated with Davutoglu's exit. FM Fidan's meeting with Hamas leadership drew Israeli fire at an awkward moment, as Trump's disarmament framework competes with Ankara's open channel to the group. The PKK amnesty bill is stalled over terms, and the Kirkuk-Ceyhan pipeline keeps flowing on borrowed legal time. Ankara is projecting power regionally, but the domestic contradictions — crackdown, inflation, fires, and an unresolved Kurdish peace process — remain as sharp as ever.
sources: Al-Monitor, Jang News, MSN, AFP/Phys.org, The Guardian, Yahoo News/LA Times, Reuters, Forbes, Business Turkey Today, Bianet, Trading Economics
